The defaults of every detector were calibrated so that false alarms are rare
on the bundled data. Real streams differ, so this vignette shows how to read
what a detector monitors, how to choose its threshold for your own data, and
how the window policy changes what it compares.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(daltoolbox)
library(heimdall)
```

## Reading the drifter output

Besides the drift decision, every detector exposes the statistic it monitors.
After `fit()`, `drifter_output` holds one row per observation; rows are `NA`
while the detector has nothing to report, for example while its window fills.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
stream <- c(rnorm(300), rnorm(300, mean = 1.5))

model <- fit(dfr_kswin(window_size = 100, stat_size = 30, seed = 1), stream)
head(model$drifter_output[95:105, ])
```

KSWIN reports the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic `D` and its p-value `p`. Plotting
the p-value on a log scale shows where the two halves of the window stop
looking alike:

```{r}
plot(model$drifter_output$p, log = "y", type = "l", xlab = "observation", ylab = "KS p-value")
abline(h = model$state$alpha, col = "red", lty = 2)
abline(v = 300, col = "blue", lty = 2)
```

The column names of each detector are listed in the README. `stealthy()`
exposes the output of its drifter in the same way, with one row per row of the
data it received.

## Calibrating a threshold

A threshold trades false alarms for detection delay. A practical way to choose
it is to run the detector, with a threshold it can never reach, on data you consider
stable, and look at the largest value its statistic reaches. A threshold above
that value keeps false alarms rare on similar data.

```{r}
set.seed(2)
stable <- data.frame(a = rnorm(1500))
no_alarm <- fit(dfr_kldist(threshold = 1e6), stable)
null_max <- max(no_alarm$drifter_output$divergence, na.rm = TRUE)
null_max
```

Then check that the change you want to catch exceeds it:

```{r}
shifted <- data.frame(a = c(rnorm(300), rnorm(300, mean = 2)))
peak <- fit(dfr_kldist(threshold = 1e6), shifted)$drifter_output$divergence
max(peak[301:400], na.rm = TRUE)
```

When the statistic of the change you care about does not rise clearly above
the stable maximum, the detector cannot separate it from noise with that
window: use a larger `window_size` (or a different detector) rather than a
lower threshold. The default `threshold = 0.12` of `dfr_kldist()` was chosen
exactly this way, for the default 100-row window.

For hypothesis-test detectors (`dfr_kswin()`, `dfr_lbdd()`, `dfr_mcdd()`), the
threshold is the significance level `alpha`. Since they test at every
observation, `alpha` must be much smaller than the usual 0.05; the defaults
are between `1e-3` and `1e-4`.

## Sliding and anchored windows

The window-based detectors (`dfr_kswin()`, `dfr_lbdd()`, `dfr_mcdd()`,
`dfr_kldist()` and `dfr_aedd()`) compare an older reference half of their
window with a recent half. `window_type` decides which data the reference
holds:

- `"sliding"` (the default) keeps the last `window_size` observations, so the
  reference moves with the stream. It detects changes relative to the recent
  past, and its memory is bounded.
- `"anchored"` keeps every observation, so the reference half stays pinned to
  the beginning of the stream. It detects changes relative to the start, and
  its memory grows with the stream.

```{r}
set.seed(3)
gradual <- seq(0, 3, length.out = 1000) + rnorm(1000, sd = 0.5)

sliding <- fit(dfr_mcdd(window_size = 100, alpha = 1e-4), gradual)
anchored <- fit(dfr_mcdd(window_size = 100, alpha = 1e-4, window_type = "anchored"), gradual)

c(sliding = sliding$drifted, anchored = anchored$drifted)
```

On this slow trend, consecutive halves of a sliding window are too similar to
reject, while the anchored reference keeps the early level and eventually
differs from the recent data. The price is memory: until a drift is reported,
the anchored window keeps every observation.

```{r}
stable <- rnorm(1000)
c(
  sliding = length(fit(dfr_mcdd(window_size = 100), stable)$state$window),
  anchored = length(fit(dfr_mcdd(window_size = 100, window_type = "anchored"), stable)$state$window)
)
```

## Speed on long streams

The window-based detectors run their test at every evaluation, which dominates
their cost. `monitoring_step` sets how many observations pass between two
evaluations:

```{r}
set.seed(4)
long_stream <- c(rnorm(3000), rnorm(1000, mean = 2))
system.time(every_step <- fit(dfr_lbdd(), long_stream))[["elapsed"]]
system.time(every_tenth <- fit(dfr_lbdd(monitoring_step = 10), long_stream))[["elapsed"]]
```

The detection is delayed by at most `monitoring_step` observations. On long
streams, also bound the memory of `stealthy()` with `history_size` and of
`nrm_memory()` with `max_size`.
